quiz.q: What happens when you call a generic function `print_area::<Circle>` and `print_area::<Square>` in the same program?
options: The compiler generates one shared function that checks the type at runtime
The compiler generates two separate monomorphized copies, one per concrete type
It fails to compile — a generic function can only be called with one type per program
Both calls run through a vtable lookup
quiz.explain: Monomorphization means the compiler stamps out a dedicated copy of the generic function for each concrete type it's called with. Calls are direct, with no runtime dispatch.

quiz.q: Why can't `Vec<T>` hold both a `Circle` and a `Square` even if both implement the same `Shape` trait?
options: Vec can only ever hold one element
Circle and Square are different concrete types, and every element of Vec<T> must be the same T
Shape must be object-safe first
Vec doesn't support custom structs
quiz.explain: Vec<T> is generic over one fixed T. Circle and Square are different types, so neither alone satisfies 'every element is T' unless you switch to a trait object like Box<dyn Shape>.

quiz.q: Why must `dyn Shape` sit behind a pointer like `Box<dyn Shape>` or `&dyn Shape`?
options: Because dyn Trait is deprecated syntax
Because dyn Shape is unsized — its size depends on the concrete type behind it, which isn't known at compile time
Because traits cannot be stored in variables at all
Because Box is required for all heap allocation in Rust
quiz.explain: Different Shape implementers have different sizes. A pointer is always a fixed size regardless of what it points to, which is what lets dyn Shape be used at all.

quiz.q: What extra information does a `Box<dyn Trait>` fat pointer carry compared to a regular pointer?
options: A copy of the trait definition source code
The address of a vtable — a table of function pointers, one per trait method, for the concrete type
The size of the Vec it lives in
A reference count
quiz.explain: A trait object pointer is 'fat': it carries the data address plus a vtable address. Calling a method looks up the right function pointer in that vtable.

quiz.q: What makes a trait NOT object-safe (unable to become `dyn Trait`)?
options: Having more than one method
Having a method with a generic type parameter, or a method returning Self by value
Having a default method
Being implemented for more than one type
quiz.explain: A vtable needs one fixed function pointer per method. A generic method would need unboundedly many versions, and a Self-returning method has an unknown size at the call site — both break the fixed-shape requirement.

quiz.q: What is the runtime cost of calling a method through `dyn Trait` compared to a generic (static dispatch) call?
options: Identical — no cost at all
One extra indirection: a vtable lookup to find the right function pointer, then a call through it
It requires garbage collection
It always allocates memory on every call
quiz.explain: Static dispatch calls the concrete function directly. Dynamic dispatch adds one vtable lookup before the jump — a small, bounded cost.

quiz.q: What does `fn make_adder(n: i32) -> impl Fn(i32) -> i32` mean?
options: The function returns a boxed trait object chosen at runtime
The function returns some fixed, unnamed concrete type implementing Fn(i32) -> i32, resolved entirely at compile time
The function can return a different closure type on each call, chosen by the caller
The function must be generic over its return type
quiz.explain: impl Trait in return position names one specific compile-time type without spelling it out. Unlike dyn Trait, every return path must produce the exact same underlying type.

quiz.q: A function has two branches, each returning a different concrete closure type, both implementing the same Fn trait. Why does `-> impl Fn(i32) -> i32` fail to compile for this function?
options: impl Trait return position requires all return paths to resolve to the identical concrete type; use Box<dyn Fn(i32) -> i32> instead
Closures can never be returned from functions
Fn traits are not object-safe
impl Trait can only be used with structs, not closures
quiz.explain: impl Trait in return position is resolved to one hidden concrete type at compile time. If the concrete type genuinely varies by branch, you need dynamic dispatch: Box<dyn Fn(i32) -> i32>.

quiz.q: You have `Vec<dyn Shape>` and get 'the size for values of type dyn Shape cannot be known at compilation time'. What's the fix?
options: Add #[derive(Sized)] to Shape
Change it to Vec<Box<dyn Shape>> so each element is a fixed-size pointer
Remove the Vec entirely, dyn Trait cannot be collected
Add a generic parameter <T: Shape> to main
quiz.explain: dyn Shape alone is unsized. Wrapping each element in Box (or &, or Rc) gives Vec a fixed-size element type to store, even though what each Box points to varies in size.

flashcards.back: The compiler generating a separate, specialized copy of a generic function for each concrete type it's called with — the basis of static dispatch.

flashcards.front: Static dispatch vs dynamic dispatch — the core trade-off.
flashcards.back: Static dispatch (generics): direct calls, no runtime cost, but one fixed type per call site. Dynamic dispatch (dyn Trait): a vtable lookup per call, but lets you mix concrete types behind one interface.
Different types implementing the trait have different sizes, so the compiler can't know dyn Trait's size at compile time. It must live behind a pointer (Box, &, Rc).
A table of function pointers, one per trait method, generated once per concrete type — what a dyn Trait fat pointer uses to dispatch a method call at runtime.

flashcards.front: What is a 'fat pointer' in the context of dyn Trait?
flashcards.back: A pointer that carries two addresses: the data itself, and the vtable for the concrete type behind it — twice the size of a normal pointer.

flashcards.front: What breaks a trait's object safety?
flashcards.back: A method with a generic type parameter, or a method that returns Self by value — both need information a fixed vtable can't provide.

flashcards.front: What does `impl Trait` in return position mean, and how does it differ from dyn Trait?
flashcards.back: It means 'some fixed concrete type implementing Trait, resolved at compile time' — no vtable, no pointer needed, but every return path must be the same underlying type (unlike dyn Trait, which can vary at runtime).

flashcards.front: When should you reach for Box<dyn Trait> instead of generics?
flashcards.back: When you need one collection or variable that can hold genuinely different concrete types behind the same trait interface, e.g. Vec<Box<dyn Shape>>.
